15771-the-bible-period-by-period-a-manua:
A Bible study manual by Josiah Blake Tidwell, born in Alabama in 1870 to a farming family. Tidwell studied at Howard College and took a master's degree from Baylor in 1903. His manual divides the Bible into periods, so students can follow the story in order. Love of neighbour, from Leviticus, guides his reading of Moses' law and Jesus' words.

Each period gets its setting, chief events, and key persons, with questions for study. The sweep runs from creation through patriarchs, kings, exile, and the early church. Tidwell writes for classes and home readers, not scholars alone. The manual still serves groups that want the Bible whole: one story, told period by period, in clear order.
19989-story-tell-lib:
Annie Trumbull Slosson wrote Story-Tell Lib in 1900, a story told in New England dialect. Lib can only hobble painfully, a few steps at a time. Her little white face is sharp and pinched, not attractive. Her eyes are faded, dull, and almost expressionless. Yet Lib is the neighborhood's beloved storyteller. Slosson builds the portrait to be overturned by Lib's gift. Listening crowds gather where her crutch stops.

Slosson specialized in the overlooked saints of village life. Her narrators are old, poor, odd, and full of grace. Dialect carries both comedy and dignity in her hands. Story-Tell Lib is among her best-loved tales. It argues that imagination sanctifies a hard life. The book is a small classic of regional fiction.
20138-true-words-for-brave-men-a-book-fo:
Charles Kingsley wrote True Words for Brave Men, a book for soldiers and sailors. Kingsley was a famed preacher and writer who loved working men. The pages quote the centurion who asked Christ to speak one word. That officer had soldiers under him and knew command from inside.

Kingsley speaks to troops in plain, warm, manly terms of faith. He links daily duty with trust in God and care for mates. Such books went into barracks and ships as gifts for servicemen. Readers get Victorian faith aimed at men who faced real danger daily.
4547-the-story-of-sonny-sahib:
Sara Jeannette Duncan, writing as Mrs. Everard Cotes, published The Story of Sonny Sahib in 1894. It opens in India in July, where a doctor tells an ayah, or Indian nurse, that her mistress lies gravely ill with fever. The household must leave by river boat for Allahabad, and the ayah must dress the sick woman, pack, and care for her baby amid heat, ruin, and fear.

From that urgent start grows the story of a small English child raised in India, caught between two worlds and two kinds of care. Duncan writes with close detail about Indian homes, servants, heat, and travel, and about the bonds that form across rank and race. Readers get a vivid late-Victorian tale of childhood, empire, and the woman who keeps a child safe when his own world falls apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atrib: Atrib was a titular see, a former bishopric kept on the books in name, in Lower Egypt. It also bore the name Athribites. The whole entry is a single line of reference. It points readers to the list of its bishops, covering the years 325 to 479, as printed in Gams on page 461. No history, bishop, or event is described beyond that pointer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crib:
This devotional entry studies the crib, or manger, where the infant Saviour lay after his birth. Properly it was the feeding place for animals in a stable or khan, likely cut from the same rock as the grotto itself. An ancient tradition places an ox and an ass beside it, echoing Isaiah and Habakkuk.

The entry treats its subject under three heads: the Basilica and Grotto of the Nativity at Bethlehem, the relics of the crib kept at St. Mary Major in Rome, and devotion to the crib. It pictures Mary and Joseph, finding no room in the inn, taking shelter in a shepherds' cave on Bethlehem's eastern hill. Pilgrims' accounts and standard works on the Holy Places support the narrative throughout.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RussoGusBackgro:
A book excerpt titled 'Loose Ends' covers the aftermath of the Cuban Missile Crisis. It follows the tense period from October 1962 to January 1963. The subjects are practical ones: verifying the Soviet withdrawal, removing the IL-28 bombers, and Kennedy's pledge not to invade Cuba. The excerpt's author is not identified in the file.

The crisis did not end when the ships turned around. Inspectors, bombers left behind, and a promise made in letters kept both governments busy for months. The excerpt treats that settlement as its story. It preserves the details of verification and withdrawal that the famous thirteen days usually crowd out, the paperwork of a war that did not happen.
nasa-tm-19670016751-studies-of-random-no:
Herbert P. Eckstein compiled this annotated bibliography at the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama in December 1966. Numbered RSIC-619, it gathers papers on random noise and the effects of noise on signals. The compilation answered a request from the Instrumentation and Communication Division at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center.

Most entries carry short annotations describing each paper. Surveys of information theory are included, since noise limits what any channel can carry. The noise treated may come from the environment, from the atmosphere or other transmitters, or from inside the equipment itself. Both Gaussian and non-Gaussian noise studies appear. Eckstein explains that the interest was in using noise usefully. Studies on eliminating noise were left out. Studies on overcoming its effects were kept, for their value to communications.
the-bible-period-by-period-a-manual-for-:
Josiah Blake Tidwell wrote a study manual dated 1916, companion to his Bible Book by Book of 1914. An introductory note praises Tidwell's guiding line from Leviticus, that one should love a neighbour as oneself. Tidwell, born in Alabama in 1870 to farmers, chaired Baylor's Bible department from 1910.

Both manuals are college-level courses in outline form, with questions at the end of each chapter to guide mastery. Tidwell studied at Howard College in Alabama, earned a master's degree at Baylor in 1903, and did further study by correspondence with Chicago. Organising the Bible by periods, rather than by single books, is this volume's method.
the-story-of-sonny-sahib:
Mrs. Everard Cotes, also known as Sara Jeannette Duncan, published this Indian tale in 1894. Chapter one finds a doctor-sahib beside a sickbed. He tells the ayah Tooni in the vernacular a hard truth. The mistress's fever is like fire. Everything must be made ready for a journey. They will go down the river by boat to Allahabad. An ox-cart must carry the mistress and baby to the bathing ghat.

Tooni is terribly frightened, and with reason. An hour earlier a ruinous crash sounded outside the hut. Guns have killed so many sahibs. The crash sent her scrambling under the bed. The doctor pulled her out by the foot. She begs to know whether there will be any more shooting, while the baby, Sonny Sahib, waits at the centre of the flight.
the-tiger-of-mysore-a-story-of-the-war-w:
G. A. Henty's Tiger of Mysore, a story of the war with Tippoo Saib published in 1895 with pictures by W. H. Margetson, begins with Henty's preface defending that war. He concedes that some Indian wars were forced on for annexation on slight provocation. The struggle with Tippoo, he argues, was different, marked by long endurance of wrong and toleration of cruelties against Englishmen and their allies. Hyder Ali, Tippoo's father, was an able conqueror who dreamed of ruling all southern India.

The chapter list promises a lost father, privateers, a rajah, a siege, a tiger in a zenana, disguise, and escape. Henty's boy hero will hunt his captive father through Tippoo's palace. Readers who like Victorian adventure with real campaigns under the fiction will find Henty's history-first approach stated honestly in his own preface.
